subject: mathematics_2a
question_text: A man has 4 sons and there are 5 schools within his reach. In how many ways can he admit his sons in the schools so that no two of them will be in the same school?

recall_prompt: Say how you would count the ways of placing four sons in five schools with no two together — why it is a permutation, and the number.
insider_note: Distinct sons into distinct schools with no sharing is an arrangement question: ⁵P₄ = 120. The first mark is the sentence that says why — different schools for different sons — not the number.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Different schools for different sons
steps.margin_note: First mark. The first son has 5 choices, the second 4 (a different school), then 3, then 2: an arrangement of 4 schools out of 5, ⁵P₄.
lines: No two sons in the same school: the 4 sons

recall.must_convey: That the four sons must get four different schools from five, which is the permutation 5 P 4.
accept: different schools for the four sons out of five so it is five P four
five choices for the first son then four then three then two
assign four different schools from five, five P four
nalugu sons ki different schools, five P four
an arrangement of four out of five

steps.why: Which son goes to which school matters, and no school is used twice, so this is an ordered choice without repetition — a permutation. It is the same count as the injections question (149.1) with sons as the domain.
common_mistakes: Using ⁵C₄ = 5, which ignores which son goes where.
Using 5⁴ = 625, which allows two sons in one school.

steps.label: Evaluate ⁵P₄

recall.must_convey: That 5 P 4 is 5 times 4 times 3 times 2 = 120.
accept: five P four is five into four into three into two which is one twenty
five four three two multiplied is one twenty
the answer is one hundred and twenty

steps.why: Four factors counting down from 5; note ⁵P₄ = ⁵P₅ = 5! because the last factor would be 1.
